title: Six Children’s Retellings of Western Classics
author: Jenna A. Robinson
summary: Jenna Robinson offers an annotated list of six children's retellings that introduce young readers to the foundational works of the Western canon and prepare them to read the originals later. The list includes Rosemary Sutcliff's retellings of the Iliad, the Odyssey, and Beowulf, Penelope Lively's retelling of the Aeneid, Margaret Hodges's picture-book version of Saint George and the Dragon from Spenser, and Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare. Each entry names the virtues or cultural references a child will meet, such as honor, duty, pietas, the Trojan horse, and the Sirens, and flags content warnings like violence or illustrated nudity. The framing draws on E.D. Hirsch's argument for cultural literacy: shared stories permeate language and equip children for wise citizenship and a lifelong enjoyment of literature. Her bottom line is that children deserve more than basic early readers, and that great stories should come early.
points: The list works as a ready reading plan for parents and classical teachers who want children to meet Homer, Virgil, Beowulf, Spenser, and Shakespeare before they can read the originals.
Hirsch's cultural literacy argument supplies the rationale: shared stories permeate our language and shape how we understand the world.
Retellings are chosen for fidelity, such as the Lambs preserving Shakespeare's phrases so children can follow the plays later.
Content warnings are given plainly, with the claim that children can handle and discern more than adults assume.
The stated aim is formation of thoughtful citizens through early exposure to what is true, good, and beautiful.
quotes: E.D. Hirsch explains in Cultural Literacy: What Every American Needs to Know that certain ideas, stories, and concepts are essential to full participation in American life. They permeate our language and shape how we understand the world.

Children who grow up with these stories are better prepared for wise citizenship and a lifelong enjoyment of great literature. And while several selections below warrant parental warnings, children can often handle more, and discern more, than adults assume.

This illustrated retelling of Homer’s Iliad brings children into a world that echoes throughout Western literature: the apple of discord, the face that launched a thousand ships, Achilles’ heel, and the Trojan horse.
By preserving many of Shakespeare’s beautiful phrases while clarifying the plots, the Lambs prepare children to listen to or watch the plays without losing the thread of the story.
Meaningful stories prepare children to read and love what is true, good, and beautiful as they get older. Good stories form thoughtful citizens and cultivate a rich literary life.
